This page will hold Part D of the first asynchronous session. The material is being prepared; check back once it is announced on Canvas.
In the meantime, here is a live code cell to confirm everything works in your browser — edit it and press Run Code:

title: Tree of Life
text:
In Part A you worked with a table of amniotes: one row per species, no structure between the rows. But those species are not an unordered bag — every one of them sits on a family tree that connects it, through shared ancestors, to every other living thing. This part is about that tree: how it is stored as data, how to draw it three ways (rectangular, round, and against a time axis), and what the words biologists use for it — clade, ancestor, divergence — mean on the screen.
Three real trees, served with this page, all from TimeTree (Kumar et al. 2022):
All code runs in your browser. The first cell may take a few seconds while Python loads.

title: Tree of Life
section: 1 · A tree is a claim about history
text:
1 · A tree is a claim about history
A phylogenetic tree has three kinds of parts, and each one asserts something:

Tips (leaves) are observed things — living species, families, classes. They are the only part anyone has ever seen.
Internal nodes are inferred ancestors: “these two lineages were once one population.” Nobody has seen one; each is a hypothesis.
Branch lengths, in the trees on this page, are time: a branch of length 6.7 means 6.7 million years of independent evolution.

Where do the trees come from? Mostly from genetics. Take the same gene from many species, line the DNA sequences up, and count differences: mutations accumulate roughly steadily, so more differences means more time since two lineages separated. That gives the shape and relative ages. To turn relative ages into millions of years, the tree is calibrated against fossils whose age and position are known. TimeTree, the source of our files, aggregates thousands of such published studies into consensus dated trees — which is why every tree here comes with real ages attached.

title: Tree of Life
section: 2 · A tree as text: the Newick format
text:
2 · A tree as text: the Newick format
Before we can draw a tree we need it as data. The standard format, Newick, writes a tree as nested parentheses: each pair of parentheses is one internal node (one ancestor), and :number after a name is the branch length. Here is one you can read by eye — humans, chimps and gorillas, with TimeTree’s ages in millions of years (Myr):
((Homo:6.7, Pan:6.7):2.2, Gorilla:8.9);
Read from the inside out: Homo and Pan each sit at the end of a 6.7-Myr branch from their shared ancestor, so the human–chimp split was 6.7 million years ago. That ancestor connects, 2.2 Myr further back, to the ancestor it shares with Gorilla — 6.7 + 2.2 = 8.9 Myr, exactly Gorilla’s own branch length. In a dated tree every tip is the same total distance from the root, because every living lineage has had the same amount of time.
The format is recursive — a tree is a node whose children are trees — so the parser is recursive too. This is the only genuinely fiddly code on the page; read it, run it, and then it is just a function we call:

title: Tree of Life
text:
3 · From text to picture
To draw a tree we give every node two coordinates. x is its total distance from the root — add branch lengths from the root down, which for a dated tree means x is time. y spreads the tips out one per row, and each ancestor sits at the mean of its children:






(One drawing trick worth stealing: instead of one ax.plot per branch — thousands of tiny artists — we collect all segments of a colour into a single line broken by None gaps and draw it in one call. Same picture, orders of magnitude faster.)
Now a real tree. This is every family of amniotes — the same group whose species table you cleaned in Part A, one level of aggregation up:


















No labels — at 956 tips they would be soup. What the shape alone shows: every mammal, bird and reptile family traces back to one node ~319 Myr ago, and the big early fork you can see near the root is mammals splitting from the reptile-plus-bird lineage. That number is not decoration; you will meet it again below, coming from a completely different file.

title: Tree of Life
section: 4 · Clades: subtrees you can point at
text:
4 · Clades: subtrees you can point at
A clade is an ancestor plus all of its descendants — a complete subtree, snapped off at one internal node. “Mammals” is a clade; “cold-blooded animals” is not, because their common ancestor also has warm-blooded descendants. Clades are the only groups a tree can actually point at, and the way to find one is through the MRCA — the most recent common ancestor of some tips you name:






Name two primate families and you get all of Primates — every family descended from the same ancestor, ~74 Myr ago:












Look at the tips before moving on: Hominidae — all great apes, including you — is one twig among nineteen. And Paleopropithecidae, the sloth lemurs, are extinct: humans arrived in Madagascar ~2,000 years ago and they were gone within a few centuries. A dated tree can carry recently-lost lineages alongside living ones.

Your turn: the carnivore clade
Cats and dogs are both carnivorans. Extract the clade containing Canidae (dogs) and Felidae (cats), draw it with labels, and print how many families it holds and how long ago their common ancestor lived.








Hint 1 — This is the primate example with two different anchor names: clade(amniotes, ["Canidae", "Felidae"]).


Hint 2 — Draw with draw_tree(carnivora, ax, labels=True, fontsize=9). You should see 16 families and an ancestor ~55 Myr back.


Fully worked solution:
carnivora = clade(amniotes, ["Canidae", "Felidae"])

print(f"{len(carnivora.leaves())} families, common ancestor "
      f"{root_age - carnivora.depth:.1f} Myr ago")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
draw_tree(carnivora, ax, labels=True, fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("Myr since the amniote root")
plt.show()
16 families from one ancestor ~55 Myr ago — and the tree answers questions the table never could. Cats’ closest relatives here are hyaenas and mongooses, not dogs; dogs sit on the other side of the very first split, nearer to bears and seals. “Cats and dogs” feel like a natural pair to us, but the clade says they have been separate lineages almost since the dinosaurs left.

title: Tree of Life
text:
5 · The round tree of life
Rectangular layout runs out of room fast: tips need vertical space, and at hundreds of tips the picture becomes a wall. The classic fix is to bend the y-axis into a circle — angle becomes tip position, radius becomes time. Same coordinates, different projection:












We colour three clades — animals, fungi, green plants — by naming two anchor tips for each, exactly as we did for primates. Everything not in a painted clade stays grey:












Three things this picture says that a list of species cannot:

Everything familiar is a wedge. All animals — sponges to humans — are one blue sector. All of Mammalia is a single tick mark.
The grey is not filler. A third of the disc is protists — algae, amoebae, ciliates, parasites. “Protist” is not a clade; it is the word for every eukaryote outside the three painted wedges, and the tree shows they do not form one group.
Fungi sit next to animals, not plants. The red and blue wedges share an ancestor long after either shared one with plants — mushrooms are, genealogically, closer to you than to anything green.

title: Tree of Life
text:
6 · The timetree of life
The round tree is for shape; a timetree puts the ages back on a readable axis. We use the phylum-level file (66 tips) and relabel the x-axis to run backwards from today, with a few reference events:






Every animal phylum was already a separate lineage before the Cambrian began — the famous “explosion” shows up here as a dense burst of splits just before 541 Mya, not after. And no branch ends at either extinction line: at phylum level, every lineage on this chart survived both of the worst catastrophes in the fossil record.
Because branch lengths are time, “when did X and Y split?” is one subtraction — the age of their MRCA:












The last line above is worth a pause: choanoflagellates, single-celled flagellates that strain bacteria out of water, split from us ~894 Mya — they are the closest living relatives of all animals, and they look remarkably like the feeding cells of a sponge.

Your turn: close the loop
In Section 3 the amniote family tree put the amniote root at 319 Myr. The eukaryote class tree is a completely different file, built from a different set of studies at a different taxonomic rank — but it contains Mammalia and Aves as tips. Use divergence to find when mammals and birds split according to this tree, and compare.








Hint 1 — The split date of a and b is the age of their MRCA: find it with clade(root, [a, b]), whose .depth is Myr since the root. Convert to “Myr ago” using the root’s age.


Hint 2 — The root’s age is the depth of any tip in a dated tree: root_age = max(l.depth for l in root.leaves()). Then return root_age - clade(root, [a, b]).depth.


Fully worked solution:
def divergence(root, a, b):
    set_depths(root)
    root_age = max(l.depth for l in root.leaves())
    return root_age - clade(root, [a, b]).depth

split = divergence(euk, "Mammalia", "Aves")
print(f"Mammalia-Aves split in the eukaryote class tree: {split:.1f} Mya")
print(f"Amniote root in the family-level file:           319.0 Mya")
Both files say 319 Myr — because the mammal–bird split is the amniote root: mammals sit on one side of the very first amniote fork and birds on the other, so “when did mammals and birds split” and “how old is the amniote common ancestor” are the same question. Two files, downloaded separately at different taxonomic ranks, agree to the decimal because TimeTree computes both from the same underlying consensus of published studies. Agreement between two views of one database is consistency; it is not independent confirmation — a distinction that matters every time two charts seem to corroborate each other.

title: Tree of Life
section: What a tree does, and does not, say
text:
What a tree does, and does not, say
Reading a phylogeny is a visual skill worth being pedantic about:

Only the nodes and branch lengths carry information. The vertical order of tips is arbitrary — every internal node can be flipped like a mobile, so “top of the chart” means nothing. Humans are not “at the end” of the tree; every living tip is exactly the same distance from the root.
The level of aggregation is part of the claim — the Part A lesson again. At phylum level no lineage dies in the great extinctions; at family level (sloth lemurs) extinction is visible everywhere. Same history, different rank, different story.
Every internal node is an inference, and some are genuinely contested — whether sponges or comb jellies split from the rest of the animals first is a live argument in the literature, and this page’s files quietly take a side. A drawn tree always looks more certain than the science behind it.

title: Tree of Life
text:
Sources and serving notes

Kumar et al. (2022) TimeTree 5: an expanded resource for species divergence times, Molecular Biology and Evolution 39:msac174 — timetree.org. Trees downloaded via “Build a Timetree” (group: Amniota at family rank; Eukaryota at class and phylum rank), Newick format, branch lengths in Myr; values unmodified.
Names with suffixes (Cebidae-1, Cebidae-2) are TimeTree’s way of serving groups that its consensus does not recover as single clades — the name is split, the tree is left honest.
Tobias et al. (2022) AVONET and Myhrvold et al. (2015) — the Part A datasets this page’s amniotes connect back to.

title: Allometry
text:
Allometry is the study of how traits scale with size. Across birds, mammals and reptiles, most size-related traits follow power laws — straight lines once both axes are logged. In this part you will draw the same allometric relationship at three levels of aggregation — individual specimens, species, and families — and watch what aggregation does to the picture.
Two real datasets, served with this page:
All code runs in your browser. The first cell may take a few seconds while Python loads.

title: Allometry
text:
1 · AVONET: one row per bird
AVONET publishes the raw measurements behind its species table: museum specimens and field captures, measured to a common protocol. We serve four of the original 26 columns — species (BirdLife taxonomy), beak length along the culmen, tarsus length, and wing length, all in millimetres.

title: Allometry
section: 2 · Cleaning: where do the rows go?
text:
2 · Cleaning: where do the rows go?
We want to plot beak length against tarsus length, which means every row we use needs both measurements (and a species name). Museum specimens are imperfect: a damaged bill or a folded skin means one trait was measured and the other was not. Count the gaps before touching anything:






Every column has holes, and they are not the same holes. Keep only the rows that can support the comparison we actually want to make:












We just discarded a fifth of the dataset. That is a legitimate cleaning step — but it is a decision, it changes what “n” means in every caption downstream, and it must be disclosed. Any figure built from this table should say 69,509 individuals, not 90,020.

title: Allometry
text:
3 · The individual level
Each point is one bird. Both axes are logged: allometry is about ratios, and a hummingbird and an ostrich need to share a readable axis.

title: Allometry
section: 4 · The groupby: from individuals to species
text:
4 · The groupby: from individuals to species
One line of code changes what a point means. groupby("species").mean() collapses every bird of a species into a single average bird:


















Averaging removed 59,000 points but the cloud barely tightened (r ≈ 0.61 → 0.62). Within-species measurement scatter is small compared to the real, ecological differences in beak shape between species — hummingbirds, finches and curlews genuinely sit in different places. Aggregation is not a magic de-noiser: it removes exactly the variation that happens within groups, no more.

Your turn: a different trait pair
Repeat the whole pipeline — cleaning included — for wing length vs tarsus length. Wing length has its own, different pattern of missing values, so start from birds, not from clean. Plot the species-level relationship and print n at each step.








Hint 1 — The subset to require is ["species", "wing_length_mm", "tarsus_length_mm"]. Beak gaps are irrelevant to this comparison — don’t drop rows for a column you aren’t using.


Hint 2 — birds.dropna(subset=...) then .groupby("species")[["wing_length_mm", "tarsus_length_mm"]].mean(), then ax.scatter(np.log10(...), np.log10(...), s=4, alpha=0.25).


Fully worked solution:
clean_w = birds.dropna(subset=["species", "wing_length_mm", "tarsus_length_mm"])
print(f"{len(birds):,} rows → {len(clean_w):,} rows")

species_w = (clean_w
             .groupby("species")[["wing_length_mm", "tarsus_length_mm"]]
             .mean())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
ax.scatter(np.log10(species_w["tarsus_length_mm"]),
           np.log10(species_w["wing_length_mm"]),
           s=4, alpha=0.25, color="#e66852")
ax.set_xlabel("log10 tarsus length (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("log10 wing length (mm)")
ax.set_title(f"Species means (n = {len(species_w):,})")
plt.show()
Wing length is missing in only ~1,100 rows, so this cleaning keeps far more data than the beak comparison did — the n you report depends on the comparison you chose. The wing–tarsus cloud is also tighter than beak–tarsus: both are limb-skeleton traits that track overall body size, while beaks track feeding ecology.

title: Allometry
section: 5 · Amniote: a table where the groupby already happened
text:
5 · Amniote: a table where the groupby already happened
The Amniote life-history database is one row per species — 21,322 of them across birds, mammals and reptiles. Somebody else already did the aggregation; what you download is the equivalent of species_means above. (In the published archive, missing values are coded -999; the copy served here has them recoded as proper missing values.)












Broad allometry: how does maximum longevity scale with adult body mass, from a 2-gram shrew to a multi-tonne crocodile? Note the cleaning step is the same decision as before — and it costs far more rows here:












Only 5,122 of 21,322 species — 24% — have both traits recorded. Missingness is not decoration in comparative databases; it is most of the table.

Your turn: one rank up
Repeat the aggregation one taxonomic rank up: collapse species into family means and redraw the mass–longevity plot. Average the logged values (a family containing a 3 kg and a 3,000 kg species should average in ratio space, not gram space).








Hint 1 — Group by two keys so each family keeps its class: pair.groupby(["class", "family"])[["log_mass", "log_longevity"]].mean(), then .reset_index() so class is an ordinary column again.


Hint 2 — Reuse the plotting pattern from the species-level chart: for cls, grp in families.groupby("class"): then ax.scatter(grp["log_mass"], grp["log_longevity"], color=class_colours[cls], label=cls). You should end up with 327 points.


Fully worked solution:
families = (pair
            .groupby(["class", "family"])[["log_mass", "log_longevity"]]
            .mean()
            .reset_index())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
for cls, grp in families.groupby("class"):
    ax.scatter(grp["log_mass"], grp["log_longevity"],
               s=18, alpha=0.7, color=class_colours[cls], label=cls)
ax.set_xlabel("family mean log10 adult body mass (g)")
ax.set_ylabel("family mean log10 maximum longevity (years)")
r_fam = np.corrcoef(families["log_mass"], families["log_longevity"])[0, 1]
ax.set_title(f"One rank up: {len(families)} families, r = {r_fam:.3f}")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()
Here aggregation does tighten the cloud: r ≈ 0.52 at species level, r ≈ 0.65 at family level, from 5,122 points down to 327. Families average away the species-level eccentrics (naked mole-rats, bats and seabirds that live far longer than their mass suggests), so the broad scaling law stands out — at the price of no longer being able to see the eccentrics, which may be exactly the species a reader cares about. Note also what carried the whole exercise: we averaged logged values. The mean of logs is the log of the geometric mean — the right average for ratio-scale traits; averaging raw grams first would let one elephant drag its whole family across the plot.

title: Allometry
section: What aggregation did, and did not, do
text:
What aggregation did, and did not, do
The relationship was “the same” at every level — log-linear, positive — but every property a reader can quote changed with the level: n went from 90,371 measurements to 69,509 usable ones, to 10,601 species, to 327 families; the correlation moved; outliers appeared and vanished. A claim made from one level does not automatically hold at another. When you caption a chart, the level of aggregation is part of the claim — say what one point is, say what n is, and say where the dropped rows went.

title: Allometry
text:
Sources and serving notes

Tobias et al. (2022) AVONET: morphological, ecological and geographical data for all birds, Ecology Letters 25:581–597. Raw individual measurements from the supplementary dataset; served here with four of 26 columns, all rows, values unmodified.
Myhrvold et al. (2015) An amniote life-history database to perform comparative analyses with birds, mammals, and reptiles, Ecology 96:3109. Served with 10 of 36 columns, all 21,322 rows; the archive’s -999 missing-value code recoded to NA. All other values unmodified.

title: The Triangle of Everything
text:
In 2023, two astrophysicists published a chart that went viral: every object in the Universe on one pair of axes — quarks, viruses, fleas, whales, planets, stars, black holes, galaxies, and the observable Universe itself (Lineweaver & Patel, All objects and some questions, American Journal of Physics 91:819). Plot mass against radius on log scales and everything that exists falls inside a triangle: one wall drawn by gravity, one wall drawn by quantum mechanics, and an apex where the two meet at the smallest possible object.
In this part you rebuild that chart step by step. Every ingredient is something you can compute: two axes, one curated table, one fact about spheres, and two famous formulas. By the end you will have drawn the figure — and you will know why it has the shape it has.
The rebuild happens in five steps:
All code runs in your browser. The first cell may take a few seconds while Python loads.

title: The Triangle of Everything
section: 1 · One pair of axes for everything
text:
1 · One pair of axes for everything
Why mass and radius? Because they are the two properties every physical object has. A virus has no temperature you can easily assign, a galaxy has no chemistry — but both have a mass and a size. If you want a chart of everything, you need axes everything can land on.
The catch is range. From a neutrino to the observable Universe, mass spans about 90 orders of magnitude and radius about 44. On linear axes, one pixel that shows the Universe would hide the entire Sun inside a region a trillion-trillion times smaller than the pixel. So both axes are logarithmic — the same move you made for allometry in Part A, stretched to its absolute limit. (We work in grams and centimetres, following the paper; on axes this wide the choice of unit just slides everything by a constant, and changes nothing about the shape.)
The chart’s raw material is a curated table — one row per object, a name, a group, a mass and a radius:












Start with five things you have an intuition for:






Notice they fall roughly on a straight line. Hold that thought — it is the key to Step 3.
First, a confession about the data. What is “the radius of a human”? The paper treats you as a sphere of radius 50 cm with mass 70 kg. Check what that implies:












Real humans are almost exactly water density; the 50-cm sphere overestimates your volume about sevenfold. On an ordinary chart that would be a scandal. Here, one decade of error is one percent of the axis — invisible. That is the quiet trade this figure makes everywhere: every value is an order-of-magnitude sketch, and at this scale that is exactly good enough. Say so in the caption, and it is honest; hide it, and it is not.

title: The Triangle of Everything
text:
2 · The full bestiary
Now all 29 objects, coloured by kind. Six groups: particles (grey), life, worlds, stars, black holes (black, naturally), and cosmic structures. The palette is colour-blind-checked, and every point carries its own label — colour alone is never the only way to tell things apart:






The interesting thing is not where the points are — it is where they aren’t. Nothing in the top-left (small but monstrously heavy), nothing in the bottom-right (huge but almost massless). Two whole corners of possibility, empty. The rest of this page explains why they must be.

title: The Triangle of Everything
section: 3 · Density is a straight line here
text:
3 · Density is a straight line here
Any object of roughly uniform density \(\rho\) obeys \(m = \frac{4}{3}\pi \rho\, r^3\). Take logs and this becomes \(\log m = 3\log r + \text{const}\) — on our axes, a straight line of slope 3, one line per density. Chemistry pins atomic matter near \(\rho \approx 1\ \text{g/cm}^3\); nuclear matter sits fourteen decades higher:






Suddenly the scatter has a skeleton. Everything made of atoms — viruses, fleas, whales, asteroids, planets, the Sun — strings out along the atomic line: that was the straight line hiding in the five familiar objects. The proton and the neutron star, fourteen decades apart in size, share the nuclear line: a neutron star really is matter at the density of an atomic nucleus, the size of a city.






Read that last line again: the least dense thing in the Universe is the Universe — about \(10^{-29}\ \text{g/cm}^3\), six protons per cubic metre.

Your turn: interrogate the densities
You have rho_all for all 29 objects. Rank everything by density and print a table from densest to fluffiest, with the group and the density of each object. Then answer from your output: which group owns the top of the table, and how many decades of density separate a red giant from a white dwarf — two objects of nearly the same mass?








Hint 1 — np.argsort(rho_all) gives indices from smallest to largest; reverse it with [::-1] to get densest first.


Hint 2 — A “decade” is a factor of ten, so the gap in decades is np.log10(rho_wd / rho_rg). Get each with rho_all[names.index("white dwarf")].


Fully worked solution:
order = np.argsort(rho_all)[::-1]

for rank, i in enumerate(order, 1):
    print(f"{rank:>2}. {names[i]:<20} {groups[i]:<18} {rho_all[i]:>9.1e} g/cm³")

gap = np.log10(rho_all[names.index("white dwarf")]
               / rho_all[names.index("red giant")])
print(f"\nred giant vs white dwarf: {gap:.0f} decades of density")
The top of the table belongs entirely to particles — the top quark and Higgs boson are the densest “objects” plotted, though for them density is a strange notion (their radius is a quantum limit, not a surface). The red giant and white dwarf differ by roughly 12 decades of density despite nearly identical masses — they are the same kind of star at two different moments of its life, which is why mass alone tells you so little and the mass–radius pair tells you so much.

title: The Triangle of Everything
text:
4 · The two walls
Now the physics that gives the chart its shape. Both walls are one-line formulas.
The gravity wall. Squeeze a mass \(m\) into a small enough radius and it becomes a black hole. That radius is the Schwarzschild radius \(r_s = 2Gm/c^2\) — for a given radius, the heaviest possible object is \(m = rc^2/2G\): slope +1 on our axes. Nothing can sit above this line: an object of that mass would already have collapsed. Black holes sit exactly on it — that is what a black hole is.
The quantum wall. Quantum mechanics denies small masses a definite tiny size: a particle of mass \(m\) cannot be localised below its Compton wavelength \(\lambda_c = \hbar / mc\), so the lightest possible object of radius \(r\) is \(m = \hbar/rc\): slope −1. Below this line, “object” stops meaning anything — try to confine a particle tighter and you create new particles instead. Fundamental particles (top quark, Higgs, electron, neutrino) are plotted on their Compton wavelengths; the composite proton gets its measured charge radius.






The empty corners of Step 2 are now explained — and shaded. They are not unexplored; they are impossible. This is the deepest trick in the figure: the absence of data is carrying the physics, and the shading turns absence into a statement.
One object deserves a second look. Check the top-right corner:












The Universe’s mass and radius satisfy the black-hole relation almost exactly. Does that mean we live inside a black hole? The paper’s answer is careful: the Schwarzschild formula assumes empty space outside the object, and outside our Hubble volume the density carries on much the same — so no. But why the numbers land on the line so precisely is the second exercise.

title: The Triangle of Everything
section: 5 · The apex, and the finished chart
text:
5 · The apex, and the finished chart
Walls of slope +1 and −1 must meet. Set them equal:
\[\frac{rc^2}{2G} = \frac{\hbar}{rc}
\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;
r = \sqrt{\frac{2G\hbar}{c^3}},\qquad
m = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar c}{2G}}.\]












The crossing point is the Planck scale — about \(10^{-33}\) cm and \(2\times10^{-5}\) g, the mass of a flea’s egg compressed to a point \(10^{20}\) times smaller than a proton. The smallest possible object is a Planck-mass black hole, which the paper calls an instanton: the only thing that is simultaneously as small as gravity allows and as small as quantum mechanics allows. Left of the Planck length, physics has no tested theory at all — the paper shades it “sub-Planckian unknown”, and so will we.
Now assemble everything — regions, walls, density skeleton, objects, apex:






That is the triangle of everything: gravity above, quantum uncertainty below, the unknown to the left, the Universe pinned to the top of the gravity wall, and every known thing strung out on density lines in between.

Your turn: put the Universe on the wall
The Universe’s point was given to you in the table. Derive it. All you need is the Hubble constant. The radius of the observable Universe is the Hubble radius \(r_H = c/H_0\); its average density is the critical density \(\rho_c = 3H_0^2 / 8\pi G\); and its mass is that density times the volume of the Hubble sphere. Then test whether your derived Universe lands on the black-hole line.








Hint 1 — r_H = c / H0, rho_c = 3 * H0**2 / (8 * np.pi * G), and the mass is density × volume of a sphere of radius r_H.


Hint 2 — m_U = 4/3 * np.pi * r_H**3 * rho_c. If your ratio is not extremely close to 1, check your powers and parentheses.


Fully worked solution:
r_H   = c / H0
rho_c = 3 * H0**2 / (8 * np.pi * G)
m_U   = 4/3 * np.pi * r_H**3 * rho_c

r_s = 2 * G * m_U / c**2
print(f"r_H = {r_H:.2e} cm   m_U = {m_U:.2e} g")
print(f"Schwarzschild radius of the Universe's mass: {r_s:.2e} cm")
print(f"ratio r_s / r_H = {r_s / r_H:.3f}")
The ratio is exactly 1 — and not by coincidence. Substitute the formulas into each other:
\[r_s = \frac{2G}{c^2}\cdot\frac{4}{3}\pi r_H^3 \cdot \frac{3H_0^2}{8\pi G}
     = \frac{r_H^3 H_0^2}{c^2}
     = r_H \left(\frac{r_H H_0}{c}\right)^2 = r_H.\]
Every constant cancels. A Universe at critical density must sit on the black-hole line, whatever the value of \(H_0\) — the “coincidence” in the chart is algebra wearing a costume. This is a lesson about reading charts, not just making them: when a data point lands suspiciously exactly on a theory line, check whether the two were secretly computed from the same ingredients.
